reason: The trunk route of New France and British Canada: sea ships to Quebec and Montreal, then bateaux and Durham boats past the rapids to Lake Ontario.

sea_head.place: Montreal (tag stadacona = Quebec is the conservative alternative)
sea_head.evidence: By the early 19th century ocean-going ships regularly berthed at Montreal, which lies just below the unnavigable Lachine Rapids; before the 1840s channel dredging the biggest ships often stopped at Quebec (tag stadacona).

river_head.place: Kingston (Cataraqui / Fort Frontenac) at the outlet of Lake Ontario
river_head.evidence: Bateaux and later Durham boats carried freight between Lachine and Kingston, the transshipment point to lake vessels; cataraqui is the lake-shore location (has_river False, gananoque is the river-flagged neighbour).

obstacles.name: Lachine Rapids
obstacles.evidence: Rapids just above Montreal harbour that stopped sea ships; goods were portaged to Lachine until the Lachine Canal opened in 1825.

obstacles.name: Cedars / Coteau rapids
obstacles.evidence: A chain of rapids at the Soulanges reach west of Montreal island, passed by small canals and tracking; tag placement medium confidence.

obstacles.name: Long Sault Rapids
obstacles.evidence: Long rapids near Cornwall that upbound bateaux had to pole or track through.

period_note: French era (1608-1763): the King's ships and merchantmen mostly unloaded at Quebec, smaller craft continued to Montreal; British era: regular ocean shipping to Montreal. Upriver traffic used bateaux from the 1760s and Durham boats from about 1800. Ottawa River (canoe fur route) deliberately excluded; the Richelieu to Lake Champlain carried bateaux but is left out as minor.

reason: Tidal to Albany; Hudson River sloops carried heavy regular traffic New York-Albany from the Dutch era on.

sea_head.evidence: Sea-going sloops and small ships sailed the tidal Hudson all the way to Albany, the head of sloop navigation.

period_note: Colonial and early US. Above Albany the Mohawk route (portage to Schenectady, bateaux and Durham boats, then the Erie Canal from 1825) is left out to keep the set minimal.

reason: Philadelphia was the largest colonial port and sloops continued to the falls at Trenton.

sea_head.evidence: Ocean ships sailed up the Delaware estuary to Philadelphia, a leading Atlantic port of the 18th century (vanilla renames shackamaxon to Philadelphia).

river_head.place: Trenton (falls of the Delaware, head of tide)
river_head.evidence: River sloops ran regularly to Trenton at the falls; Durham boats brought flour and iron down from Easton to Philadelphia.

period_note: Colonial and early US (1680s-1837). Durham boat traffic above Trenton to Easton was seasonal and is not included.

reason: Added: sea sloops and brigs regularly sailed to Middletown and Hartford for the West Indies trade throughout the colonial era.

sea_head.place: Hartford (Middletown, tag nehantuck, is the intermediate port)
sea_head.evidence: Colonial Hartford and Middletown were river ports trading directly with the West Indies by sea-going vessels.

period_note: 1640s-1837. Flatboats above Enfield Falls to Springfield and beyond were minor and seasonal; not included. Optional river if the set must stay very small.

reason: Shallow and rocky; traffic was downstream-only arks and rafts on spring freshets, and rapids above Port Deposit blocked sea access.

sea_head.place: Havre de Grace / Port Deposit (mouth on Chesapeake Bay)
sea_head.evidence: Sea craft reached only the mouth at the head of Chesapeake Bay; rapids begin just above Port Deposit.

reason: Tidal Potomac carried sea ships to Alexandria and Georgetown, major tobacco and flour ports.

sea_head.place: Alexandria (Georgetown on the opposite bank is tag anacostia)
sea_head.evidence: Ocean ships loaded tobacco and flour at Alexandria and Georgetown, the head of tidewater below the Little Falls.

period_note: Colonial and early US. The Patowmack Canal (1802) let boats past Great Falls toward Cumberland, but only in high water; excluded. The lower reach is mostly estuary, so the channel adds little beyond coast.

reason: Sea ships to Richmond at the fall line; James River bateaux hauled tobacco regularly between Lynchburg and Richmond.

sea_head.evidence: Tidewater shipping reached Richmond, the port where upriver tobacco was inspected and shipped.

river_head.evidence: From the 1770s hundreds of bateaux carried tobacco hogsheads from Lynchburg down to Richmond, the regular trade until the canal replaced them around 1840.

obstacles.name: Falls of the James
obstacles.evidence: Fall line at Richmond between tidewater and the bateau reach, bypassed by a canal from the 1790s.

period_note: Colonial and early US (1610s-1837); bateau era about 1770-1840.

reason: Seaport Savannah plus regular pole-boat (Petersburg boat) cotton and tobacco traffic to Augusta at the fall line.

sea_head.evidence: Savannah, a short way up the river, was the colonial and cotton seaport of Georgia (vanilla renames tybee to Savannah).

river_head.evidence: Petersburg boats and other pole boats carried cargo between Augusta and Savannah in the late 18th and early 19th centuries.

period_note: 1733-1837; steamboats on the Savannah from about 1816.

reason: The central artery of French/Spanish Louisiana and the US interior: sea ships to New Orleans, keelboats and later steamboats to St. Louis.

sea_head.evidence: Ocean ships crossed the bars at the passes and sailed about 150 km upriver to New Orleans, the port of the whole basin.

river_head.place: St. Louis (Natchez, tag natchez, on the way)
river_head.evidence: Keelboats and bateaux worked New Orleans-Natchez-St. Louis from the 18th century and steamboats made it routine after 1817.

head.evidence: Flatboats and keelboats ran from Pittsburgh down the Ohio to New Orleans from the 1780s; the Falls at Louisville were the only barrier.

head.place: Kansas City / Westport landing (Fort Osage and Independence nearby)
head.evidence: Keelboats supplied Fort Osage from 1808 and steamboats ran regularly to the Independence-Westport landings by the 1830s, the start of the Santa Fe trade.
The Great Raft made Natchitoches the head of navigation, a French trading post supplied by boat from New Orleans since 1714.

obstacles.name: Falls of the Ohio
obstacles.evidence: Rapids at Louisville, the only barrier between Pittsburgh and New Orleans, bypassed by the Louisville and Portland Canal from 1830.

period_note: French 1699-1763, Spanish 1763-1803, US after. Ohio traffic from the 1780s; Missouri regular only after about 1808 (fur posts) and 1819+ (steam), so it is the weakest branch; Red River branch tag calcasieu sits in natchitoches_province (confidence medium-low). Upper Mississippi above St. Louis (lead mines, Prairie du Chien) left out.

river: Rio de la Plata / Parana / Paraguay
reason: The colonial link between Buenos Aires and Paraguay: river sailing craft carried yerba mate, tobacco and timber regularly via Santa Fe and Corrientes to Asuncion.

sea_head.evidence: Ocean ships anchored in the shallow roads of Buenos Aires (deep-draught ones at Montevideo or Ensenada); the city sits on the border of ituzaingo and tuvicha_mini on the map, so the tag is medium confidence.

river_head.place: Asuncion (Santa Fe = qom_caia on the way)
river_head.evidence: Balandras and other river vessels sailed regularly between Buenos Aires, Santa Fe, Corrientes and Asuncion, the main outlet for Paraguayan yerba mate.

head.evidence: River vessels reached Salto, where the Salto Grande falls closed navigation; Paysandu and Concepcion del Uruguay lie on the way.

period_note: Colonial from the 1580s (Santa Fe 1573, Buenos Aires 1580); traffic interrupted by the Paraguayan isolation under Francia (1814-1840). Upper Parana above Corrientes (Jesuit missions, Apipe rapids) left out. Uruguay head tag: Salto city itself falls on the mandisobi side on the map (confidence medium-low).

reason: Portuguese Amazonia's only highway: regular convoys of large decked sail-and-oar boats carried cacao and forest goods between Belem, Santarem, Obidos and Barra.

sea_head.evidence: Ocean ships from Lisbon traded at Belem on the Para estuary; the city falls between samauma and mairi on the map.

river_head.place: Manaus (Barra do Rio Negro); Santarem = tupulicus and Obidos = obidos on the way
river_head.evidence: Barra do Rio Negro, capital of the captaincy of Sao Jose do Rio Negro from 1791, was supplied from Belem by river boats; steamers came only in 1853.

period_note: Portuguese colonial (1616-1822) and imperial Brazil. The craft (canoas de negocio, cobertas, igarites) were large planked sailing boats, not dugout canoes, but this is the borderline case against the canoe rule; drop if the set must be strict. Belem is technically on the Para/Tocantins estuary, not the Amazon mainstem.

reason: Sea-going schooners and brigs sailed up to Angostura, the port of Spanish Guayana and Bolivar's base.

sea_head.place: Angostura (Ciudad Bolivar, formerly Santo Tomas de Guayana)
sea_head.evidence: Angostura at the narrows of the Orinoco was reached by sea vessels and exported cattle products and tobacco of the llanos.

period_note: Angostura founded 1764 (earlier Santo Tomas lower down). Lancha traffic up the Apure to San Fernando de Apure existed but is left out as minor.

reason: The trunk route of New Granada: champanes (large poled cargo barges) carried goods Cartagena-Mompox-Honda for Bogota throughout the colonial era.

sea_head.place: River mouth at Bocas de Ceniza / Barranquilla
sea_head.evidence: A sand bar kept sea ships out of the mouth; sea cargo came in via Cartagena and the Canal del Dique (tags calamari, mahates) or via Santa Marta.

river_head.evidence: Honda at the rapids was the colonial river port where goods for Bogota left the champanes; Mompox was the main intermediate port.

period_note: 1530s-1837; steam concession 1825 but steamers irregular before the 1840s. Canal del Dique (1582) joined Cartagena to the river near Calamar (tag mahates) but silted often; it is a canal, not added as a branch.

reason: Guayaquil was the Pacific shipyard and port of the Audiencia of Quito, and river boats ran regularly to Babahoyo (Bodegas), the start of the road to Quito.

sea_head.evidence: Sea ships sailed up the Guayas estuary to Guayaquil, the main port and shipyard of the colonial Pacific coast.

river_head.evidence: Cargo moved by river craft on the Babahoyo to the Bodegas warehouses, where the mule road to Quito began.

period_note: 1540s-1837. Short reach (about 70 km); drop if the set must be very small.

reason: Paulo Afonso falls split it; the lower reach was a short bar-bound stretch for small coasters and the middle reach had only local barca traffic before steamers in the 1870s.

sea_head.evidence: Small coastal vessels reached Penedo just inside the mouth.

reason: Dutch plantation rivers with only short tidal reaches; the Essequibo is blocked by rapids above Bartica and shipping stayed at the coast.

sea_head.evidence: Sea ships loaded at the plantation landings near the river mouths.

reason: Historically important (bongos carried Peru silver and goods from the Chagres mouth to Venta de Cruces), but the EU5 map has no river there (chuchures has_river False).

sea_head.evidence: Sea ships unloaded at the mouth, then bongos and chatas poled up to Cruces for the mule road to Panama.

period_note: Added as a candidate and excluded only because there is no map river to use.

reason: Hudson's Bay Company ships reached Fort Vancouver regularly only from 1825, too short a span within the game period.

sea_head.evidence: HBC supply ships sailed up the Columbia to Fort Vancouver from 1825.

period_note: Excluded; could be reconsidered if the 1825-1837 fur trade matters.

reason: Colonial traffic was small; the cotton steamboat trade to Montgomery only began in the 1820s.

sea_head.evidence: Mobile was the seaport at the head of Mobile Bay.

period_note: Excluded; late (1820s-1830s) steamboat river. If added, the head would be Montgomery (tag atahachi).
